topics.title: RIVET: CKB-native GitHub backup using IPFS, RGB++, and CCC

recent_posts.topic_title: RIVET: CKB-native GitHub backup using IPFS, RGB++, and CCC
recent_posts.author: Jedi_dtechmaker
recent_posts.content_text:
Hello everyone,
I am building RIVET, a decentralized developer platform that backs up, timestamps, and restores your entire GitHub history using CKB, IPFS, and RGB++.
Developers currently build their entire careers and reputations on platforms they do not actually control. This is not just about suspensions. It is about hacks, lost passwords, losing access to an old email, or sudden policy changes. Rivet ensures that no matter what happens, your code, commit history, and proof of authorship are permanently secured, cryptographically provable, and fully restorable.
The Problem
Developers rent their reputation on Web2 platforms:
· GitHub can suspend your account overnight, deleting years of open source contributions with no appeal process.
· There is no native cryptographic proof of authorship. Git commits and timestamps are trivially easy to forge.
· If you lose your account for any reason, you lose your contribution graph and your proof of work.
Rivet fixes this by providing an insurance policy for your code, built natively on CKB.
What Rivet Is
A decentralized backup and identity platform that:
· Mirrors your entire GitHub history (every branch, tag, and commit) to IPFS and Arweave.
· Anchors a cryptographic proof (Merkle root) to a CKB Cell for immutable timestamping.
· Issues a Sovereign Passport (an RGB++ Spore DOB) that proves your developer identity and history on chain.
· Allows you to restore all your repositories to a brand new GitHub account, perfectly preserving your original commit timestamps and authorship.
How It Works
· Data Layer: git clone --mirror creates full backup bundles.
· Storage Layer: Bundles are uploaded to IPFS (via Helia) for hot access, and eventually Arweave for permanent cold storage.
· Proof Layer: A Merkle tree is computed from your commit hashes.
· Anchor Layer: The Merkle root is submitted to CKB as a Timestamp Cell.
· Application Layer: A Next.js UI allows you to browse your backed up code, diffs, and commits seamlessly.
Why CKB Shapes the Design
Everything in Rivet relies on CKB’s unique architecture:
· Timestamp Cells: We use CKB’s Cell model to store Merkle roots. Because Cells are immutable once confirmed, they provide absolute proof that a specific codebase existed at a specific time.
· Spore DOBs (RGB++): Your Sovereign Passport is implemented as a Spore DOB. It is an on chain resume containing your total commits, languages, and backup history that you actually own.
· CCC Integration: We use @ckb-cccckb-ccc/co@ckb-ccce and @ckb-ccc/connector-react for passwordless authentication and transaction signing. Your wallet is your developer account.
Current Status (POC Phase)
What is Working:
· Next.js Web Platform.
What is Not Yet Done:
· CCC Wallet connection and passwordless authentication.
· GitHub OAuth integration to fetch repositories.
· Native file tree browser and commit history viewer (reading original timestamps)
· PostgreSQL database schema mapping users to CKB addresses
· Git bundle generation and IPFS uploading
· Merkle root computation and CKB transaction building
· RGB++ Spore DOB minting
· CLI Restore tool (for pushing back to GitHub)
Tech Stack
Layer Technology
Runtime Node.js + Fastify
Frontend Next.js 14 + React 1@ckb-ccc
Blockchain @ckb-ccc/core + RGB++ Spore Protocol
Storage IPFS (Helia) + Arweave
Database PostgreSQL
Git Engine isomorphic-git
Key Design Decisions
Decision Reasoning
CCC Wallet Auth No passwords. Your CKB address is your permanent identity.
Next.js (SSR) Public developer profiles need to be SEO friendly so recruiters and auditors can index them.
IPFS + Arweave IPFS provides fast retrieval for the web UI. Arweave acts as a permanent insurance layer.
Merkle Trees Instead of storing thousands of commit hashes on chain (too expensive), we anchor a single Merkle root.
Features Planned for v1
The Sovereign Passport
Mint an RGB++ Spore DOB that updates with every backup. It acts as an on chain, verifiable resume that third parties can cryptographically verify.
The Restore Wizard
If you lose access to your GitHub for any reason, the Restore Wizard downloads your IPFS bundle, uses git-filter-repo to remap your old emails to a new one, and pushes everything to a new GitHub account. Your contribution graph lights up exactly as it was, with historical dates intact.
Public Verifier
A dedicated page where auditors or employers can paste a CKB transaction hash and cryptographically verify that a developer’s claimed code history is mathematically genuine.
Fiber Payments (Future)
Once the identity layer is established, Fiber Network will route bounty and sponsorship payments directly to the developer’s new account, using their RGB++ Passport as the escrow proof.
Build Order
· Phase 1: Foundation (Current): Web UI, CCC auth, GitHub repo viewer.
· Phase 2: Backup Engine: Git mirroring, IPFS storage, CKB Merkle anchoring.
· Phase 3: Sovereign Passport: Spore DOB minting and public profiles.
· Phase 4: Restore CLI: Email remapping and GitHub push automation.
· Phase 5: Social Features: Stars, forks, code search, and discovery.
Questions for the Community
1. As a developer, would a decentralized backup for your GitHub history give you peace of mind?
2. What features would you consider essential for the v1 Restore process?
3. CKB Capacity: I plan to batch multiple repositories into a single Merkle tree to save on CKB capacity when anchoring. Has anyone established best practices for batching proofs in Timestamp Cells?
4. Spore DOBs: Any concerns with constantly updating a Spore DOB with new backup stats? Is it better to mint a new DOB per year, or continually mutate one?
Links
Temporary Live Demo (Vercel): DEMO
Architecture Doc: Rivet/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md at main · jedi-dtechmaker/Rivet · GitHub
Looking for feedback. Thanks for reading!

recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program | Fiber Weir — Condition-Gated Payment Streams for Fiber Network
recent_posts.author: Carl
recent_posts.content_text:
Spark Program | Fiber Weir — Condition-Gated Payment Streams for Fiber Network
1. Project Overview
Project name: Fiber Weir
One-sentence summary: A working implementation of a piece of Fiber Network’s own named roadmap item — “programmable conditional payment” — letting a payment stream continue only while an on-chain-verifiable condition holds true, halting and refunding automatically the instant it doesn’t, instead of relying on a party manually confirming delivery.
Category: Protocol-level infrastructure / primitive, with a working reference implementation (not a consumer app) — the same category as prior successfully-funded infra work in this program (Cross-Chain Hub extensions, zk-Lock, CKB-VM validation).
2. Team Profile
Core member: Carl — solo developer, project lead and sole contributor.
Repo: [github.com/oxdev6/fiber-weir]
Contact: Discord: carlcn6 · Email: carll67788@gmail.com · Telegram: carl6 · GitHub: @oxdev6
3. Project Background
Fiber Network’s own repository lists, among its stated roadmap items, “programmable conditional payment” — explicitly covering PTLC, hold-invoice application protocols, on-chain contract conditions, and agent fair exchange. This is not an inferred gap; it is the core team’s own, current, public statement of unfinished work, in the same category of evidence that has already grounded successful projects in this program.
Today, Fiber’s hold-invoice mechanism gates payment release on one thing only: whether the payee can reveal a preimage matching a hash committed at invoice creation. This is a secret-knowledge gate — it proves someone knows a number, not that anything specific actually happened. For a streaming payment — pay-per-API-call, pay-per-compute-cycle, pay-per-second of metered service — this means “was the service actually delivered correctly” is left to manual confirmation, off-chain trust, or ad hoc application logic bolted on top. There is no way, today, for the payment mechanism itself to enforce “only continue paying while this on-chain-verifiable condition holds.”
A related, already-live project, AgentPay, gives AI agents wallets and uses Fiber’s existing hold-invoice mechanism to “lock funds until service delivery is confirmed.” Read precisely, “confirmed” there still means a party or process revealing a preimage once it believes delivery happened — the same secret-knowledge mechanic, wrapped in an agent-friendly SDK. AgentPay does not implement on-chain contract conditions, and does not claim to; it is application-layer plumbing built on top of the existing primitive. This project builds the primitive itself — the thing a future AgentPay, or any other consumption-side Fiber application, could build on top of, rather than another application sitting beside it.
This project is explicitly infrastructure, not an application competing for the same attention as another payment gateway or checkout flow. The program’s own recent public guidance (the August 2026 “What Spark Is Not” post) names a specific complaint: too many Fiber submissions sit on the “value circulation side” — another payment entry point — rather than giving Fiber new underlying capability. This project sits on neither side by itself: it is the missing primitive underneath both, demonstrated with one concrete reference implementation to prove it works, not pitched as a consumer product in its own right.
4. Solution
A conditional TLC (time-locked contract) extension: a payment stream where each installment’s release depends on both the existing preimage check and a matched, verifiable condition observation. If the condition stops matching, or the stream reaches its expiry block without a fresh release, the stream halts and unreleased funds become refundable — no manual dispute, no trusted third party confirming delivery after the fact.
Pre-grant work already completed and unit-tested: the off-chain rules governing this — exactly when a release is valid, when a proof is stale, when refund unlocks, how terminal states lock, how predicate commitments are computed and validated at construction — are implemented as a pure state machine (ConditionalPaymentStream) with twelve enforcement claims individually tested. This is the hardest design work: getting the boundary conditions right (freshness, monotonicity, the exact expiry/refund handoff, overflow safety) before any of it touches real infrastructure.
What this grant funds — the part that turns a tested state machine into an enforced protocol feature: none of the above is enforced anywhere yet. There is no conditional branch in Fiber’s actual on-chain lock script, no verifier that observes real CKB state and feeds it into the state machine, no wire schema carrying conditional payment data between peers, and no feature-bit negotiation so peers can even agree to attempt one. The state machine currently governs nothing but its own unit tests. This grant funds the specific, scoped work of connecting it to reality: the on-chain script enforcement, the live verifier, and the wire integration — plus an honestly-scoped RPC surface, SDK, and demo built on top once that connection exists.
Reference implementation, to prove the connected system concretely: a pay-per-successful-API-response stream, where each response batch is signed and the on-chain predicate verifies that signature before a release is permitted.
Named and deferred, not hidden: watchtower support for conditional streams and full state persistence across node restarts are real, non-trivial pieces of work explicitly out of scope for this grant, tracked as future work rather than assumed safe. Concretely, this means the reference implementation and its testnet demonstration are scoped to a channel that stays open and online for the duration of the demo — force-close-mid-stream safety for conditional payments is a known, currently-unresolved gap, named here rather than glossed over.
5. Technical Approach
Stack: Rust, extending nervosnetwork/fiber’s commitment-lock script (in fiber-scripts/contracts/) and crates/fiber-lib/fiber-types directly; TypeScript SDK and a minimal dashboard frontend. Any CKB-side address/cell handling in the SDK or demo frontend uses CCC (CKBers’ Codebase), the current standard — not Lumos, which the ecosystem has officially deprecated.
Current layered state, precisely:
Layer 5: Demo Frontend — NOT BUILT (basic dashboard scaffold exists, no live data)
Layer 4: Client SDK — NOT BUILT
Layer 3: RPC Extension — NOT BUILT
Layer 2: Wire/Actor Integration — NOT BUILT (no conditional fields in TLC/invoice wire types, no feature bit, no conditional branch in the payment actor)
Layer 1: On-chain Lock Script — NOT BUILT (no conditional branch in commitment-lock; no live verifier connecting real CKB state to the state machine)
Layer 0: Off-chain State Machine — DONE. ConditionalPaymentStream (crates/fiber-types/src/conditional.rs), 12/20 enforcement claims implemented and unit-tested per GROUND_TRUTH.md
Ground-truth discipline, already established and to be maintained throughout: the repo’s GROUND_TRUTH.md distinguishes, claim by claim, what’s actually enforced from what’s merely designed — this project continues that discipline rather than abandoning it once funding starts. Every claim that flips from “not implemented” to “implemented” during the grant gets its enforcement pointer and passing test linked in the same file, and docs/fiber-cond-roadmap.md is kept current as the scoped work proceeds.
The actual technical work this grant funds — the project’s own defined integration boundary, not a paraphrase:
“This repository currently contains Fiber’s TLC/hold-invoice settlement machinery but does not contain the active, modifiable fiber-scripts contract work needed to enforce a new arbitrary predicate during force-close. This slice deliberately keeps the contract adapter explicit rather than pretending local Rust validation is on-chain enforcement.”
The remaining integration work, in the project’s own words, and in this order of dependency:
Add a versioned CommitmentLock witness variant carrying the predicate commitment.
Add the conditional fields to the invoice/TLC wire schemas with a compatibility/version bit.
Implement the CKB verifier adapter and use it before RemoveTlcFulfill.
Update the watchtower settlement witness and deployed testnet script configuration.
Add a two-node integration test against the upgraded contract.
Honest scoping of item 4 specifically: items 1, 2, 3, and 5 are the committed scope of this grant — they take the already-tested state machine from “validated in isolation” to “enforced on-chain and exercised end-to-end between two real nodes,” which is the core claim of this proposal. Item 4 (the watchtower settlement witness update) is the one item most likely to exceed a 6-week/$1,000 solo scope on top of the other four, and is treated as a best-effort stretch goal, not a committed deliverable — attempted if items 1–3 and 5 land with time to spare, explicitly deferred to follow-on work otherwise. Either way, the demo and its safety claims are scoped to a channel that remains open for the duration of testing; force-close-mid-stream safety is not claimed unless item 4 is actually completed and demonstrated.
Testnet only, never mainnet, within this grant’s scope — the “deployed testnet script configuration” in item 4 refers strictly to Fiber’s existing testnet deployment, not a new mainnet migration.
Item 6, once 1–3 and 5 are real: expose create_conditional_stream/get_stream_status/cancel_stream over RPC, wrap them in a TypeScript SDK, and build the reference pay-per-API-response demo on top, including its failure path.
Explicitly out of scope, stated upfront, per the project’s own stated boundary for this slice: PTLC cryptography, a general oracle framework beyond signature-verification predicates, and — per the existing scope note in the repo — routing, multi-part payments (MPP), UDTs, and trampoline payments, all intentionally excluded from this first slice.
Highest technical risk, named directly: items 1–3 above are exactly the class of work Fiber’s own team has spent significant effort hardening in the existing (non-conditional) settlement path — adding a new branch to a live lock script and the payment actor without introducing a fund-safety regression is real risk, not a formality. Mitigations carried over from the original design and still binding:
No edits to the existing commitment-lock script or payment actor before a written summary of their current behavior exists (docs/existing-settlement-flow.md).
New logic is additive (a new branch/field), never a modification of existing non-conditional paths, so a bug in the new code cannot regress today’s working hash-lock payments.
A named adversarial test matrix — stale proof, future-dated proof, expiry-boundary release, refund-before-expiry attempt, duplicate/replayed proof, terminal-state re-entry — extending the unit tests already passing in the state machine to the newly-connected on-chain and wire layers.
Force-close mid-stream is explicitly not claimed safe in this grant, per the watchtower gap named in Section 4 — the adversarial matrix covers correctness of the state machine and its on-chain enforcement while a channel is open, not the dispute path, which remains future work.
Devnet-only until the full matrix passes; testnet only for the final demo recording; no mainnet within this grant’s scope.
Explicitly out of scope, stated upfront: PTLC cryptography, a general oracle framework beyond signature-verification predicates, watchtower support for conditional streams, and full state persistence across restarts.
6. To-Do List (6-week plan)
Starting point, precisely: the off-chain state machine (ConditionalPaymentStream) is implemented and unit-tested. The remaining work is the project’s own defined integration boundary — five items, with a sixth (RPC/SDK/demo) once those land.
Week 1 (done, pre-grant): Off-chain state machine and its unit tests; GROUND_TRUTH.md, docs/fiber-cond.md, docs/fiber-cond-roadmap.md established as the project’s ongoing honesty discipline.
Week 2: Item 1 — versioned CommitmentLock witness variant carrying the predicate commitment, unit-tested in isolation against the script.
Week 3: Item 2 — conditional fields added to invoice/TLC wire schemas with a compatibility/version bit. Item 3 begins — CKB verifier adapter construction. Milestone 1.
Week 4: Item 3 completed — verifier adapter wired in and used before RemoveTlcFulfill. Item 5 — two-node integration test against the upgraded contract, run to passing on devnet. Milestone 2.
Week 5: Item 4 attempted as a best-effort stretch goal (watchtower settlement witness + testnet script config update) — committed to follow-on work if it doesn’t land cleanly alongside the rest. Item 6 begins: RPC layer and fiber-weir-sdk.
Week 6: Reference demo completed (signed API-response provider + dashboard), including the on-camera failure-path demonstration on testnet. GROUND_TRUTH.md updated to reflect final, honest claim status — including item 4’s actual outcome, whichever way it went. Milestone 3.
7. Required Funding & Breakdown
Requested amount: $1,000 (standard cap for a single technical project).
Structure: 20% upfront on approval, remainder released against three milestones, each independently verifiable without a full code review.
Upfront — $200 (20%): released on grant approval.
Milestone 1 — Witness variant + wire schema + verifier underway — $300: due end of Week 3. Trigger: item 1 (CommitmentLock witness variant) complete and unit-tested; item 2 (wire schema fields + version bit) complete; item 3 (verifier adapter) under active construction. Verification: reviewer runs the provided test command and sees pass/fail output directly.
Milestone 2 — Verifier live, two-node integration passing — $350: due end of Week 4. Trigger: item 3 complete (verifier used before RemoveTlcFulfill), item 5 complete (two-node integration test passing on devnet). Verification: reviewer watches the recorded two-node test run; GROUND_TRUTH.md’s diff is visible in commit history, claim by claim.
Milestone 3 — RPC, SDK, demo, honest final ground truth — $150: due end of Week 6. Trigger: item 6 (RPC/SDK/demo) complete, reference demo recorded (happy path and failure path) on testnet, and GROUND_TRUTH.md/fiber-cond-roadmap.md updated to reflect exactly what shipped — including item 4’s actual, honestly-reported outcome. Verification: reviewer watches the two demo videos and runs the SDK example themselves.
8. Deliverables + How to Verify
Deliverables:
Public repo (already live: github.com/oxdev6/fiber-weir), MIT-licensed, with GROUND_TRUTH.md maintained claim-by-claim throughout the grant, not just at the start.
Conditional branch added to the real commitment-lock CKB script, unit-tested.
Live verifier connecting real CKB chain state to the existing, already-tested ConditionalPaymentStream state machine.
Wire schema additions (TLC/invoice conditional fields, feature bit) and the conditional branch in the payment actor.
fiber-weir-sdk TypeScript package with a runnable example.
Reference demo (signed API-response provider + dashboard) demonstrating a live conditional stream on testnet, including a deliberate on-camera failure-path demonstration.
How to verify (no code review required):
Read GROUND_TRUTH.md’s diff across the grant period directly — each claim’s status change is tied to a specific commit and test, which is a stronger, more precise verification method than a general code review.
Run the on-chain script’s and state machine’s test suites directly — pass/fail output is self-evident.
Watch the recorded multi-node adversarial test run for Milestone 2.
Watch the two demo videos (happy path, failure path) for Milestone 3, and run the SDK example against local nodes.
9. Current State vs. Funded Work
Current state, precisely: repo live at github.com/oxdev6/fiber-weir. The off-chain state machine (ConditionalPaymentStream) is implemented and unit-tested — commitment matching, mismatched-observation rejection, expiry-triggered refund, and double-release/double-refund prevention on terminal states are all covered. In the project’s own words: “this slice deliberately keeps the contract adapter explicit rather than pretending local Rust validation is on-chain enforcement.” That is the honest line this proposal stands on.
What’s explicitly not built yet: the five-item integration boundary in Section 5 — no CommitmentLock witness variant, no wire schema fields, no live verifier, no watchtower settlement update, no two-node integration test. A node today can exercise the state machine’s logic in isolation; it cannot enforce a conditional payment against a real peer or real chain state.
Funded scope: items 1, 2, 3, and 5 of that integration boundary as committed deliverables, item 4 (watchtower) as a named best-effort stretch goal, and item 6 (RPC/SDK/demo) once the rest is real — all detailed week-by-week in Section 6.
Explicitly out of scope, named rather than hidden: PTLC cryptography, a general oracle framework beyond signature-verification predicates, routing/MPP/UDTs/trampoline payments (per the project’s own existing scope note), and — unless item 4 is actually completed — force-close-mid-stream safety for conditional payments.
10. CKB / Fiber Alignment
This project does not use Fiber as a convenient payment rail for an unrelated idea — it directly implements a named piece of Fiber’s own roadmap (“programmable conditional payment… on-chain contract conditions”), using CKB’s Turing-complete script model to make the condition itself arbitrary and verifiable, not just a clock or a shared secret. It is infrastructure, not another application competing on the same “circulation side” the program has explicitly said it has enough of — it is the missing layer underneath the next generation of consumption-side Fiber applications (metered APIs, agent-to-agent commerce, pay-per-compute services), proven with one concrete, honestly-scoped reference implementation rather than promised in the abstract.

4. Solution

A conditional TLC (time-locked contract) extension: a payment stream where each installment’s release depends on both the existing preimage check and a matched, verifiable condition observation. If the condition stops matching, or the stream reaches its expiry block without a fresh release, the stream halts and unreleased funds become refundable — no manual dispute, no trusted third party confirming delivery after the fact.

Pre-grant work already completed and unit-tested: the off-chain rules governing this — exactly when a release is valid, when a proof is stale, when refund unlocks, how terminal states lock, how predicate commitments are computed and validated at construction — are implemented as a pure state machine (ConditionalPaymentStream) with twelve enforcement claims individually tested. This is the hardest design work: getting the boundary conditions right (freshness, monotonicity, the exact expiry/refund handoff, overflow safety) before any of it touches real infrastructure.

What this grant funds — the part that turns a tested state machine into an enforced protocol feature: none of the above is enforced anywhere yet. There is no conditional branch in Fiber’s actual on-chain lock script, no verifier that observes real CKB state and feeds it into the state machine, no wire schema carrying conditional payment data between peers, and no feature-bit negotiation so peers can even agree to attempt one. The state machine currently governs nothing but its own unit tests. This grant funds the specific, scoped work of connecting it to reality: the on-chain script enforcement, the live verifier, and the wire integration — plus an honestly-scoped RPC surface, SDK, and demo built on top once that connection exists.

Reference implementation, to prove the connected system concretely: a pay-per-successful-API-response stream, where each response batch is signed and the on-chain predicate verifies that signature before a release is permitted.

Named and deferred, not hidden: watchtower support for conditional streams and full state persistence across node restarts are real, non-trivial pieces of work explicitly out of scope for this grant, tracked as future work rather than assumed safe. Concretely, this means the reference implementation and its testnet demonstration are scoped to a channel that stays open and online for the duration of the demo — force-close-mid-stream safety for conditional payments is a known, currently-unresolved gap, named here rather than glossed over.

5. Technical Approach

Stack: Rust, extending nervosnetwork/fiber’s commitment-lock script (in fiber-scripts/contracts/) and crates/fiber-lib/fiber-types directly; TypeScript SDK and a minimal dashboard frontend. Any CKB-side address/cell handling in the SDK or demo frontend uses CCC (CKBers’ Codebase), the current standard — not Lumos, which the ecosystem has officially deprecated.

Current layered state, precisely:

Layer 5: Demo Frontend       — NOT BUILT (basic dashboard scaffold exists, no live data)
Layer 4: Client SDK          — NOT BUILT
Layer 3: RPC Extension       — NOT BUILT
Layer 2: Wire/Actor Integration — NOT BUILT (no conditional fields in TLC/invoice wire types, no feature bit, no conditional branch in the payment actor)
Layer 1: On-chain Lock Script — NOT BUILT (no conditional branch in commitment-lock; no live verifier connecting real CKB state to the state machine)
Layer 0: Off-chain State Machine — DONE. ConditionalPaymentStream (crates/fiber-types/src/conditional.rs), 12/20 enforcement claims implemented and unit-tested per GROUND_TRUTH.md

Ground-truth discipline, already established and to be maintained throughout: the repo’s GROUND_TRUTH.md distinguishes, claim by claim, what’s actually enforced from what’s merely designed — this project continues that discipline rather than abandoning it once funding starts. Every claim that flips from “not implemented” to “implemented” during the grant gets its enforcement pointer and passing test linked in the same file, and docs/fiber-cond-roadmap.md is kept current as the scoped work proceeds.

The actual technical work this grant funds — the project’s own defined integration boundary, not a paraphrase:

“This repository currently contains Fiber’s TLC/hold-invoice settlement machinery but does not contain the active, modifiable fiber-scripts contract work needed to enforce a new arbitrary predicate during force-close. This slice deliberately keeps the contract adapter explicit rather than pretending local Rust validation is on-chain enforcement.”

The remaining integration work, in the project’s own words, and in this order of dependency:

  1. Add a versioned CommitmentLock witness variant carrying the predicate commitment.
  2. Add the conditional fields to the invoice/TLC wire schemas with a compatibility/version bit.
  3. Implement the CKB verifier adapter and use it before RemoveTlcFulfill.
  4. Update the watchtower settlement witness and deployed testnet script configuration.
  5. Add a two-node integration test against the upgraded contract.

Honest scoping of item 4 specifically: items 1, 2, 3, and 5 are the committed scope of this grant — they take the already-tested state machine from “validated in isolation” to “enforced on-chain and exercised end-to-end between two real nodes,” which is the core claim of this proposal. Item 4 (the watchtower settlement witness update) is the one item most likely to exceed a 6-week/$1,000 solo scope on top of the other four, and is treated as a best-effort stretch goal, not a committed deliverable — attempted if items 1–3 and 5 land with time to spare, explicitly deferred to follow-on work otherwise. Either way, the demo and its safety claims are scoped to a channel that remains open for the duration of testing; force-close-mid-stream safety is not claimed unless item 4 is actually completed and demonstrated.

Testnet only, never mainnet, within this grant’s scope — the “deployed testnet script configuration” in item 4 refers strictly to Fiber’s existing testnet deployment, not a new mainnet migration.

Item 6, once 1–3 and 5 are real: expose create_conditional_stream/get_stream_status/cancel_stream over RPC, wrap them in a TypeScript SDK, and build the reference pay-per-API-response demo on top, including its failure path.

Explicitly out of scope, stated upfront, per the project’s own stated boundary for this slice: PTLC cryptography, a general oracle framework beyond signature-verification predicates, and — per the existing scope note in the repo — routing, multi-part payments (MPP), UDTs, and trampoline payments, all intentionally excluded from this first slice.

Highest technical risk, named directly: items 1–3 above are exactly the class of work Fiber’s own team has spent significant effort hardening in the existing (non-conditional) settlement path — adding a new branch to a live lock script and the payment actor without introducing a fund-safety regression is real risk, not a formality. Mitigations carried over from the original design and still binding:

  • No edits to the existing commitment-lock script or payment actor before a written summary of their current behavior exists (docs/existing-settlement-flow.md).
  • New logic is additive (a new branch/field), never a modification of existing non-conditional paths, so a bug in the new code cannot regress today’s working hash-lock payments.
  • A named adversarial test matrix — stale proof, future-dated proof, expiry-boundary release, refund-before-expiry attempt, duplicate/replayed proof, terminal-state re-entry — extending the unit tests already passing in the state machine to the newly-connected on-chain and wire layers.
  • Force-close mid-stream is explicitly not claimed safe in this grant, per the watchtower gap named in Section 4 — the adversarial matrix covers correctness of the state machine and its on-chain enforcement while a channel is open, not the dispute path, which remains future work.
  • Devnet-only until the full matrix passes; testnet only for the final demo recording; no mainnet within this grant’s scope.

Explicitly out of scope, stated upfront: PTLC cryptography, a general oracle framework beyond signature-verification predicates, watchtower support for conditional streams, and full state persistence across restarts.

6. To-Do List (6-week plan)

Starting point, precisely: the off-chain state machine (ConditionalPaymentStream) is implemented and unit-tested. The remaining work is the project’s own defined integration boundary — five items, with a sixth (RPC/SDK/demo) once those land.

  • Week 1 (done, pre-grant): Off-chain state machine and its unit tests; GROUND_TRUTH.md, docs/fiber-cond.md, docs/fiber-cond-roadmap.md established as the project’s ongoing honesty discipline.
  • Week 2: Item 1 — versioned CommitmentLock witness variant carrying the predicate commitment, unit-tested in isolation against the script.
  • Week 3: Item 2 — conditional fields added to invoice/TLC wire schemas with a compatibility/version bit. Item 3 begins — CKB verifier adapter construction. Milestone 1.
  • Week 4: Item 3 completed — verifier adapter wired in and used before RemoveTlcFulfill. Item 5 — two-node integration test against the upgraded contract, run to passing on devnet. Milestone 2.
  • Week 5: Item 4 attempted as a best-effort stretch goal (watchtower settlement witness + testnet script config update) — committed to follow-on work if it doesn’t land cleanly alongside the rest. Item 6 begins: RPC layer and fiber-weir-sdk.
  • Week 6: Reference demo completed (signed API-response provider + dashboard), including the on-camera failure-path demonstration on testnet. GROUND_TRUTH.md updated to reflect final, honest claim status — including item 4’s actual outcome, whichever way it went. Milestone 3.

7. Required Funding & Breakdown

  • Requested amount: $1,000 (standard cap for a single technical project).

  • Structure: 20% upfront on approval, remainder released against three milestones, each independently verifiable without a full code review.

  • Upfront — $200 (20%): released on grant approval.

  • Milestone 1 — Witness variant + wire schema + verifier underway — $300: due end of Week 3. Trigger: item 1 (CommitmentLock witness variant) complete and unit-tested; item 2 (wire schema fields + version bit) complete; item 3 (verifier adapter) under active construction. Verification: reviewer runs the provided test command and sees pass/fail output directly.

  • Milestone 2 — Verifier live, two-node integration passing — $350: due end of Week 4. Trigger: item 3 complete (verifier used before RemoveTlcFulfill), item 5 complete (two-node integration test passing on devnet). Verification: reviewer watches the recorded two-node test run; GROUND_TRUTH.md’s diff is visible in commit history, claim by claim.

  • Milestone 3 — RPC, SDK, demo, honest final ground truth — $150: due end of Week 6. Trigger: item 6 (RPC/SDK/demo) complete, reference demo recorded (happy path and failure path) on testnet, and GROUND_TRUTH.md/fiber-cond-roadmap.md updated to reflect exactly what shipped — including item 4’s actual, honestly-reported outcome. Verification: reviewer watches the two demo videos and runs the SDK example themselves.

8. Deliverables + How to Verify

Deliverables:

  • Public repo (already live: github.com/oxdev6/fiber-weir), MIT-licensed, with GROUND_TRUTH.md maintained claim-by-claim throughout the grant, not just at the start.
  • Conditional branch added to the real commitment-lock CKB script, unit-tested.
  • Live verifier connecting real CKB chain state to the existing, already-tested ConditionalPaymentStream state machine.
  • Wire schema additions (TLC/invoice conditional fields, feature bit) and the conditional branch in the payment actor.
  • fiber-weir-sdk TypeScript package with a runnable example.
  • Reference demo (signed API-response provider + dashboard) demonstrating a live conditional stream on testnet, including a deliberate on-camera failure-path demonstration.

How to verify (no code review required):

  • Read GROUND_TRUTH.md’s diff across the grant period directly — each claim’s status change is tied to a specific commit and test, which is a stronger, more precise verification method than a general code review.
  • Run the on-chain script’s and state machine’s test suites directly — pass/fail output is self-evident.
  • Watch the recorded multi-node adversarial test run for Milestone 2.
  • Watch the two demo videos (happy path, failure path) for Milestone 3, and run the SDK example against local nodes.

9. Current State vs. Funded Work

  • Current state, precisely: repo live at github.com/oxdev6/fiber-weir. The off-chain state machine (ConditionalPaymentStream) is implemented and unit-tested — commitment matching, mismatched-observation rejection, expiry-triggered refund, and double-release/double-refund prevention on terminal states are all covered. In the project’s own words: “this slice deliberately keeps the contract adapter explicit rather than pretending local Rust validation is on-chain enforcement.” That is the honest line this proposal stands on.
  • What’s explicitly not built yet: the five-item integration boundary in Section 5 — no CommitmentLock witness variant, no wire schema fields, no live verifier, no watchtower settlement update, no two-node integration test. A node today can exercise the state machine’s logic in isolation; it cannot enforce a conditional payment against a real peer or real chain state.
  • Funded scope: items 1, 2, 3, and 5 of that integration boundary as committed deliverables, item 4 (watchtower) as a named best-effort stretch goal, and item 6 (RPC/SDK/demo) once the rest is real — all detailed week-by-week in Section 6.
  • Explicitly out of scope, named rather than hidden: PTLC cryptography, a general oracle framework beyond signature-verification predicates, routing/MPP/UDTs/trampoline payments (per the project’s own existing scope note), and — unless item 4 is actually completed — force-close-mid-stream safety for conditional payments.

10. CKB / Fiber Alignment

This project does not use Fiber as a convenient payment rail for an unrelated idea — it directly implements a named piece of Fiber’s own roadmap (“programmable conditional payment… on-chain contract conditions”), using CKB’s Turing-complete script model to make the condition itself arbitrary and verifiable, not just a clock or a shared secret. It is infrastructure, not another application competing on the same “circulation side” the program has explicitly said it has enough of — it is the missing layer underneath the next generation of consumption-side Fiber applications (metered APIs, agent-to-agent commerce, pay-per-compute services), proven with one concrete, honestly-scoped reference implementation rather than promised in the abstract.

recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program | CKB Builder Lab: Interactive Developer Onboarding Infrastructure for the CKB Ecosystem
recent_posts.author: devnash
recent_posts.content_text:
Thank you for the detailed final evaluation and recommendations. I understand that the main gap identified is not the technical implementation of CKB Builder Lab, but the lack of structured and quantitative evidence demonstrating its educational effectiveness.
I agree with the recommendations and will focus on implementing a structured developer user-testing process with clearly defined tester profiles, standardized learning tasks, pre-test and post-test knowledge assessments, task completion times, error rates, completion rates, drop-off points, and structured feedback.
Where practical, I will also include a comparison group using existing CKB documentation to provide a baseline for evaluating learning outcomes.
The results will be compiled into an Educational Effectiveness Report covering the methodology, anonymized user-testing data, learning-score changes, task performance, user difficulties, and key findings. I will then use these findings to make targeted improvements to the onboarding experience and challenges.
This will allow us to move beyond qualitative feedback and provide measurable evidence of whether CKB Builder Lab improves understanding of the CKB Cell Model and reduces the barrier to entry for new developers.
I appreciate the committee’s feedback and will use these recommendations to strengthen the project and make future evaluation more rigorous and evidence-based.

Proof-of-Inquiry Gateway for CKB
Developer / Team
RadhikaChain / RadhikaChain Research
Independent open-source engineering project focused on verifiable agent infrastructure, blockchain interoperability, privacy-preserving evidence, and machine-to-machine services.
Project Description
We are building an open-source Proof-of-Inquiry (PoI) infrastructure for AI agents and blockchain services.
The system allows an agent to request an operation, collect evidence from multiple sources, verify the resulting state, and produce a cryptographic proof that the operation was executed under a defined policy without requiring all underlying private data to be published.
The CKB-focused prototype will implement a CKB evidence/attestation layer that connects PoI receipts with CKB transactions/cells and provides a reproducible verification interface for agents.
The project will use Rust where appropriate and expose the resulting capabilities through structured APIs/MCP-compatible interfaces.
The prototype is intentionally scoped as an infrastructure and verification project rather than a token speculation or trading project.
CKB Ecosystem Relevance
The project will provide an open-source verification interface that allows agents and CKB applications to consume verifiable cross-chain/process evidence.
The prototype will explore:
CKB-native anchoring of PoI commitments;
verification of external evidence through CKB cells/transactions;
reproducible Rust tooling;
agent-facing discovery and verification interfaces;
Bitcoin and RadhikaChain evidence references;
privacy-preserving commitments instead of publishing sensitive source data.
This creates a reusable infrastructure component that can be consumed by CKB applications, wallets, agent systems, and Web5 services.
Deliverables
Open-source PoI-to-CKB adapter.
Rust verification library.
CKB testnet demonstration.
PoI evidence schema.
CKB commitment/attestation schema.
Agent/MCP-compatible verification API.
Reproducible deployment package.
Automated integration tests.
Security and failure-mode documentation.
Bilingual technical documentation.
Public GitHub repository.
Online demonstration.
Validation Plan
The prototype will be tested against:
valid evidence;
modified evidence;
replayed evidence;
invalid CKB transaction references;
inconsistent commitments;
service restart;
network interruption;
duplicated requests.
The goal is to demonstrate that invalid evidence is rejected deterministically while valid evidence remains independently verifiable.
Estimated Timeline
8 weeks.
Weeks 1–2
CKB adapter architecture, schemas, Rust interfaces, PoI mapping.
Weeks 3–4
CKB anchoring and verification implementation.
Weeks 5–6
Agent/MCP interface, testnet deployment and automated validation.
Weeks 7–8
Security testing, documentation, demo, public release and user feedback.
Funding Requested
Up to $2,000 equivalent.
Suggested allocation:
$600 — development and integration infrastructure;
$400 — testing and deployment environments;
$300 — CKB testnet/integration tooling;
$300 — security and verification testing;
$200 — documentation/demo infrastructure;
$200 — user testing and feedback.
Expected Outcome
At completion, the ecosystem will have a working open-source prototype demonstrating how an agent can request verification, obtain a PoI commitment, anchor relevant evidence to CKB, and independently verify the result.
The project will provide reusable infrastructure rather than a closed application.
Long-Term Direction
The prototype can later evolve toward:
CKB ↔ Bitcoin evidence;
CKB ↔ RadhikaChain verification;
agent-to-agent machine payments;
RWA evidence;
privacy-preserving compliance proofs;
decentralized agent infrastructure.
These are future directions and are not required for the initial Spark deliverable.

中英文技术文档；
公开 GitHub 仓库；
在线演示。

8 周。
申请资金
最高 $2,000 等值资金，用于开发、测试、部署、验证、安全测试、文档及用户反馈。

项目完成后，将形成一个可公开验证的开源原型，使 Agent 能够：

  • 使用 commitment，而不是公开敏感原始数据。

该基础设施可以被 CKB 应用、钱包、Agent 系统以及 Web5 服务复用。

交付成果

  1. 开源 PoI-to-CKB adapter；

  2. Rust verification library；

  3. CKB Testnet demonstration；

  4. PoI evidence schema；

  5. CKB commitment/attestation schema；

  6. Agent/MCP verification API；

  7. 可复现部署环境；

  8. 自动化集成测试；

  9. 安全和故障处理文档；

  10. 中英文技术文档；

  11. 公开 GitHub 仓库；

  12. 在线演示。

计划周期

8 周。

申请资金

最高 $2,000 等值资金，用于开发、测试、部署、验证、安全测试、文档及用户反馈。

预期成果

项目完成后，将形成一个可公开验证的开源原型，使 Agent 能够：

请求验证
→ 获得 PoI commitment
→ 在 CKB 上锚定相关证据
→ 独立验证最终结果。

长期方向

未来可以扩展到：

Bitcoin ↔ CKB
CKB ↔ RadhikaChain
Agent-to-Agent machine payments
RWA evidence
privacy-preserving compliance proofs
decentralized agent infrastructure

以上扩展不是本次 Spark 第一阶段的必要交付内容。

recent_posts.topic_title: Proof of Buy，一种专为Layer1设计的Layer2共识
recent_posts.author: Lawliet_Chan
recent_posts.content_text:
一种来自L1的审查攻击 及 防御手段
前文提到，在proof of buy中，我们在finalize L2 block的时候，会将这些L2 block header上传到L1上去。
但这迎来一个问题， 不管L1有多去中心化， 但具体在某个高度出块的时候， 一般而言总是只有一个矿池出的块最终被采纳的。 在这种情况下， 此刻出块的L1矿工，就具备对L2 block审查的权力， 具体而言，他自己可能就是既是L1的矿工也参与L2的挖矿，此时恰逢他自己在L1出块，他可以选择拒绝接收 那些goal比他还高的L2 block， 只打包他自己在L2出的块。
这种攻击方式无法随着L1的去中心化而降低被审查的风险，因为每个矿池都可能为了自己的利益选择拒绝某些L2 block。 长此以往， L2 的finalize 将会被L1的所有矿工所拿捏。
防御手段
84365af82f97a728133cb089d29e94c02232×1482 215 KB
我们可以做如下变动：
上传L2 block header到L1的时候， 不能明文上传，只能上传Commitment，这样L1矿工看不到具体内容便无法进行审查
当L1打包了所有 L2 矿工发来的 commitment并出块之后，L2 矿工将自己在L1 block上被打包签名的这些 commitment 在L2网络里广播出来，并证明这些commitment 在L1的某个block上可以查到的并且是自己生成的，很简单，只需要 open(block_header, random) = commitment， 这是所有L2全节点都可以验证出来的。
如此， 就可以在防止被L1审查的情况下 让 L1 帮助完成finalize L2 block了。
这里可以继续强调一下，L1帮助L2 finalize有个很大的好处是：防止L2被长程攻击和自私挖矿攻击
